title: Smart Business Idioms
summary: Learn two common business expressions to talk about agreement and estimates. These phrases will help you sound natural in meetings.

sections.p: When people are on the same page, they share the same understanding or goals about a project. It means everyone agrees and knows what to do next. We often use this phrase in meetings to check if the team has the same idea before starting work.

ex.en: Let's review the schedule so we are all on the same page.
ex.mean: Let's check the plan so we all agree.

ex.en: Before we start the project, I want to make sure we are on the same page.
ex.mean: I want to be sure we share the same plan.

sections.p: A ballpark figure is a rough, general estimate or a guessed number. You use it when you do not have the exact details yet, but you want to give a general idea of a cost or time. A ballpark figure helps people understand the scale of something quickly.

ex.en: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the new website design?
ex.mean: Can you give me a rough cost estimate?

ex.en: I do not have the final numbers, but a ballpark figure is five thousand dollars.
ex.mean: I have a rough guess of five thousand dollars.

tip: Imagine standing in a baseball stadium (a ballpark) trying to guess the score, or all reading the exact same page in a book together to remember these idioms!

quiz.en: We need to talk before the meeting to ensure we are on the ___.
Could you give me a ___ for how much this repair will cost?

quiz.ask: What does 'on the same page' mean?
quiz.en: To be on the same page means to...
Which sentence uses the idioms correctly?
choices: I gave my boss a ballpark figure because I did not know the exact price.
We are on the same page of the restaurant menu.
She wrote a ballpark figure on the whiteboard to read a story.

quiz.en: Let's have a quick call to make sure everyone is on the same ___.
